speech1-q01.college: Two speakers produce acoustically distinct tokens of the same word, and listeners identify both correctly. Which core problem must a theory of speech perception account for?
speech1-q01.simple: Two people say the same word, but the sounds are physically different. Listeners still hear the same word both times. What puzzle does this show?

speech1-q02.college: In a synthesis experiment, vocal-tract resonance is altered while the excitation source is held constant. Which acoustic property is most directly manipulated?
speech1-q02.simple: A computer voice keeps the same buzz (the source) but changes how the mouth shape rings (resonance). What is really being changed?

speech1-q03.college: A student interprets each dark horizontal band in a vowel spectrogram as a distinct syllable. Which correction accurately describes what the bands represent?
speech1-q03.simple: A vowel's sound image shows several dark sideways bands. A student says each band is its own syllable. What should the student be told?

speech1-q04.college: A synthetic /u/ has low F1 and low F2. If F2 is shifted while the source is held constant, which comparison does this manipulation permit?
speech1-q04.simple: A computer-made /u/ has low F1 and low F2 (the first two resonance bands). If only F2 is moved and the buzz stays the same, what can we learn?

speech1-q05.college: Inverse filtering removes the estimated vocal-tract filter and leaves a buzz-like source signal. Why is applying a new filter to that source still informative?
speech1-q05.simple: Taking away the mouth's shaping (the filter) leaves only a buzz. Why is it still useful to add a new filter to that buzz?

speech1-q06.college: Tokens of two vowels form overlapping clouds in F1 by F2 space. Which conclusion does this overlap support?
speech1-q06.simple: On a chart of F1 against F2, the dots for two vowels spill into each other. What does that tell us?

speech1-q07.college: What methodological advantage do synthesized /b/, /d/, /g/ formant transitions offer over recordings of three distinct natural syllables?
speech1-q07.simple: Why use computer-made /b/, /d/, /g/ sounds instead of just recording three real syllables?

speech1-q08.college: Stimuli are spaced in equal F2-onset steps. Pair A straddles the labeling boundary, and pair B falls within one category at the same acoustic separation. What is the purpose of this comparison?
speech1-q08.simple: The sounds change in equal steps of F2 at the start. Pair A sits on two sides of the line between labels. Pair B sits on one side, with the same size gap. Why compare these two pairs?

speech1-q09.college: An identification task yields three peaked response regions because participants select among /b/, /d/, and /g/. Why is this result by itself insufficient to demonstrate categorical perception?
speech1-q09.simple: People pick /b/, /d/, or /g/ for each sound, and the answers form three clear humps. Why is that not enough to show categorical perception (hearing sounds in sharp groups)?

speech1-q10.college: Suppose a noncategorical listener is uniformly sensitive to equal F2 differences across the continuum. Which discrimination function does this predict?
speech1-q10.simple: Imagine a listener who notices equal F2 changes equally well anywhere along the set of sounds. How well should that listener tell pairs apart?

speech1-q11.college: Identification shifts sharply at two locations, and discrimination of equally spaced pairs peaks at those same locations. Which interpretation is best supported?
speech1-q11.simple: Labels flip quickly at two spots, and people tell equal-gap pairs apart best at those same two spots. What is the best reading of this?

speech1-q12.college: Two listeners place their category boundaries at different stimulus steps. Which analysis best preserves the theoretical comparison between boundary and discrimination?
speech1-q12.simple: Two listeners put the line between sound groups at different steps. What is the best way to analyze their results?

speech1-q13.college: In the shortened class discrimination task, every pair is physically different. Why can a same response nonetheless be informative?
speech1-q13.simple: In the short class test, the two sounds in every pair are really different. Why does it still mean something when someone answers same?

speech1-q14.college: How could reduced within-category discrimination be advantageous for speech recognition?
speech1-q14.simple: How could being worse at hearing differences inside one sound group actually help us understand speech?

speech1-q15.college: In a high-amplitude sucking paradigm, sucking declines across repeated sounds and then increases after a new token. What does this recovery most directly indicate?
speech1-q15.simple: A baby sucks less as the same sound repeats, then sucks more when a new sound plays. What does that jump back up mainly show?

speech1-q16.college: Infants show greater sucking recovery after a change that crosses a category boundary than after an equal-sized within-category change. Which finding does this parallel?
speech1-q16.simple: Babies suck harder again after a sound change that crosses into a new group than after an equal change inside one group. What result does this match?

speech1-q17.college: English-learning infants become less accurate over development on a contrast that is used in Hindi but not in English. Which interpretation is consistent with perceptual narrowing?
speech1-q17.simple: English-learning babies get worse with age at hearing a sound difference that Hindi uses but English does not. What does perceptual narrowing (hearing tuned to your own language) say about this?

speech1-q18.college: Adults show sharp identification and boundary-aligned discrimination for plucked and bowed nonspeech sounds. Which claim does this result directly challenge?
speech1-q18.simple: Adults sort plucked and bowed sounds (not speech) into sharp groups and hear differences best at the line between them. Which idea does this go against?

speech1-q19.college: Trained chinchillas produce categorical-like responses along a VOT continuum of speech sounds. Which conclusion follows?
speech1-q19.simple: Trained chinchillas sort speech sounds along a VOT range (the delay before voicing starts) into groups, much like people do. What does that tell us?

speech1-q20.college: A difficult nasal contrast becomes more discriminable with relevant infant experience. How does this finding extend the perceptual narrowing account?
speech1-q20.simple: A hard-to-hear difference between nasal sounds gets easier for babies who hear it in their language. What does this add to the idea of narrowing?

speech2-q01.college: Which observation most directly contradicts a model in which lexical processing begins only after phoneme decisions are complete?
speech2-q01.simple: Some models say word recognition starts only after each speech sound is fully decided. Which finding argues most clearly against that?

speech2-q02.college: A strict phoneme threshold transmits an identical /b/ output for every token on one side of the boundary. What does this predict about downstream effects of those tokens?
speech2-q02.simple: A strict cutoff sends the same /b/ signal for every sound on one side of the line. What should that mean for the steps that come after?

speech2-q03.college: A model continuously transmits partial acoustic activation forward but contains no top-down connections. How should this architecture be classified?
speech2-q03.simple: A model keeps passing partly finished sound information forward, but nothing flows back down. What kind of model is this?

speech2-q04.college: Which property of the furniture chain makes it an analogy for thresholded processing?
speech2-q04.simple: What about the furniture chain makes it an example of threshold processing (all-or-nothing passing of information)?

speech2-q05.college: A drought immediately affects interconnected levels of a food web while population sizes continue to change. Which processing property does this analogy illustrate?
speech2-q05.simple: A drought right away changes linked levels of a food web, while animal numbers keep shifting. What does this example show about processing?

speech2-q06.college: What is the rationale for recording eye movements while participants click on bear or pear?
speech2-q06.simple: Why track where people look while they click on bear or pear?

speech2-q07.college: McMurray observes step-like final identification alongside graded competitor fixations. Which conclusion is compatible with both results?
speech2-q07.simple: McMurray finds that final clicks jump sharply from one word to the other, while looks to the other word change slowly. What idea fits both results?

speech2-q08.college: Two tokens are both identified as bear, but the token closer to the boundary elicits more fixations on pear. Which variable differs between the tokens?
speech2-q08.simple: People click bear for both sounds. The sound closer to the line gets more looks at pear. What is different between the two sounds?

speech2-q09.college: Under a cascaded model, how should competitor fixations change as a token moves toward the category boundary from inside the category?
speech2-q09.simple: In a cascade model (information flows on before it is finished), what should happen to looks at the other word as a sound moves closer to the line?

speech2-q10.college: A bilabial stop near the boundary provides partial support for both /b/ and /p/. How can pear draw fixations before the participant clicks bear?
speech2-q10.simple: A lip sound near the line partly fits both /b/ and /p/. How can pear get looks before the person clicks bear?

speech2-q11.college: The nonword Beace primes war, and the nonword ging primes queen. What accounts for the effectiveness of these nonword primes?
speech2-q11.simple: Hearing the made-up word Beace speeds up war, and ging speeds up queen. Why do these fake words help at all?

speech2-q12.college: Why does categorical identification fail to demonstrate a thresholded mapping from phonemes to words?
speech2-q12.simple: People give sharp, all-or-nothing labels. Why does that not prove that sounds must be fully decided before words are found?

speech2-q13.college: Which connection specifically constitutes top-down lexical feedback?
speech2-q13.simple: Which link counts as lexical feedback (a backward link in the model)?

speech2-q14.college: What is the purpose of comparing word to nonword continua in which the lexical item favors opposite phoneme interpretations?
speech2-q14.simple: Why compare two sets of sounds where the real word sits at opposite ends?

speech2-q15.college: A student claims Ganong simply found a general increase in word responses and disregards where the identification curves diverge. Which evidence does this overlook?
speech2-q15.simple: A student says Ganong just found more word answers overall and ignores where the curves split apart. What is the student missing?

speech2-q16.college: A lexically driven boundary-shift account predicts the largest effect at which positions on the continuum?
speech2-q16.simple: If word knowledge moves the line between sounds, where along the set of sounds should the effect be biggest?

speech2-q17.college: Ganong's identification curves diverge mainly in the transition region. Which account does this pattern support?
speech2-q17.simple: Ganong's curves split apart mostly in the middle, where the sound changes from one to the other. What idea does that pattern back up?

speech2-q18.college: In TRACE, the final /g/ strongly favors plug over blood and blush. Through what mechanism can it influence the ambiguous onset?
speech2-q18.simple: In TRACE, the last sound /g/ strongly favors plug over blood and blush. How can it change how the unclear first sound is heard?

speech2-q19.college: Which processing demand distinguishes spoken input in TRACE from a static display of a written word?
speech2-q19.simple: What makes speech input in TRACE harder to handle than a written word that sits still on a page?

speech2-q20.college: An onset competitor attracts early fixations that decline as the target's ending arrives. What does this cohort effect demonstrate?
speech2-q20.simple: A word that starts the same way gets early looks, and then fewer looks once the end of the real word is heard. What does this cohort effect show?

aphasias-q01.college: A patient comprehends a spoken word but has difficulty repeating it verbatim. Why did disconnection models treat this dissociation as informative?
aphasias-q01.simple: A patient understands a heard word but has trouble saying it back word for word. Why did disconnection models find this useful?

aphasias-q02.college: Fluent output contains neologisms and paraphasic substitutions, and comprehension is impaired. Which distinction prevents equating fluent speech with intact language?
aphasias-q02.simple: A patient talks smoothly but uses made-up words and swapped words, and understands poorly. Why does smooth talk not mean normal language?

aphasias-q03.college: A patient omits function words and grammatical particles but retains major content words. What does the term telegraphic characterize?
aphasias-q03.simple: A patient leaves out small grammar words but keeps the main content words. What does the word telegraphic describe?

aphasias-q04.college: Why is it misleading to treat Broca's original patients as prototypical cases under every later definition of Broca's aphasia?
aphasias-q04.simple: Why is it wrong to treat Broca's first patients as perfect examples of every later meaning of Broca's aphasia?

aphasias-q05.college: Why are lemma selection and positional-level processing important to the grammar and lexicon proposal?
aphasias-q05.simple: Why do lemma selection (picking the word) and the positional step matter for the idea that grammar and words are separate?

aphasias-q06.college: Why assess comprehension in a patient whose speech is agrammatic and accompanied by motor impairment?
aphasias-q06.simple: A patient speaks without grammar and also has trouble moving the mouth. Why test how well the patient understands?

aphasias-q07.college: A patient correctly matches the dog bit the man to the matching drawing. Why does this not demonstrate intact syntactic processing?
aphasias-q07.simple: A patient picks the right drawing for the dog bit the man. Why does that not show the patient's grammar is fine?

aphasias-q08.college: For the dog that the man is biting is angry, which interpretation depends on computing the sentence's structural relations?
aphasias-q08.simple: In the dog that the man is biting is angry, which meaning can only be found by working out the sentence structure?

aphasias-q09.college: Why include reversible and implausible center-embedded sentences in addition to semantically constrained ones?
aphasias-q09.simple: Why test sentences where either noun could do the action, or where the event is unlikely, along with sentences where meaning gives the answer?

aphasias-q10.college: Broca-type patients have particular difficulty when syntax conflicts with probable thematic roles, whereas Wernicke-type patients perform poorly across conditions. What motivated the original inference?
aphasias-q10.simple: Broca-type patients struggle most when grammar goes against the likely roles. Wernicke-type patients do poorly on almost everything. What did this first lead researchers to think?

aphasias-q11.college: Why replace a broad clinical description such as poor comprehension with controlled task contrasts?
aphasias-q11.simple: Why swap a broad label like poor comprehension for careful comparisons between tasks?

aphasias-q12.college: For it's the cat that the dog is biting, participants must identify the agent. Which response reflects syntactic analysis rather than a first-noun heuristic?
aphasias-q12.simple: For it's the cat that the dog is biting, people must say who is doing the biting. Which answer follows the grammar instead of just picking the first noun?

aphasias-q13.college: Object clefts and passives are more difficult than active sentences for patient groups. What must an adequate explanation account for?
aphasias-q13.simple: Patient groups find object clefts and passives harder than plain active sentences. What does a good explanation have to cover?

aphasias-q14.college: Healthy undergraduates under time pressure or memory load show similar vulnerability to complex sentence types. Which explanation does this support?
aphasias-q14.simple: Healthy college students who are rushed or holding things in memory have the same trouble with hard sentence types. Which explanation does this back up?

aphasias-q15.college: Saygin compares verbal and nonverbal versions of action and object matching. Why keep the action relation constant while varying its presentation format?
aphasias-q15.simple: Saygin has patients match actions and objects using words or using pantomime (acted-out actions). Why keep the same action link but change how it is shown?

aphasias-q16.college: Performance on nonverbal action matching correlates with lesions involving Broca's area. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
aphasias-q16.simple: Doing poorly on action matching without words goes along with damage to Broca's area. What is the best reading of this?

aphasias-q17.college: A patient has difficulty matching both spoken words and meaningful environmental sounds to drawings. Which common processing demand should be considered?
aphasias-q17.simple: A patient has trouble matching both spoken words and meaningful everyday sounds to drawings. What job do both tasks share?

aphasias-q18.college: Deficits in both verbal and nonverbal sound matching are associated with damage to posterior language regions. Why integrate behavioral and lesion-mapping evidence?
aphasias-q18.simple: Trouble matching both words and other sounds goes along with damage toward the back of the language areas. Why put the task results and the brain damage results together?

aphasias-q19.college: Which research approach most directly advances the debate between grammar-specific and general-processing accounts?
aphasias-q19.simple: Which kind of study helps most in deciding whether the problem is grammar itself or general thinking resources?

aphasias-q20.college: Voxel-based lesion mapping associates anterior damage with broad fluency deficits and posterior damage with broad comprehension deficits. Which claim is appropriate to this level of measurement?
aphasias-q20.simple: Voxel-based mapping (linking small spots of brain damage to scores) ties front damage to broad fluency problems and back damage to broad understanding problems. What claim fits how rough these measures are?

development1-q01.college: Why does the generativity of language pose a problem for a stored-list account of acquisition?
development1-q01.simple: Why is generativity (making endless new sentences) a problem for the idea that children just store a list of sentences?

development1-q02.college: Which finding would most directly undermine the claim that reinforcement of grammatical utterances is sufficient to teach grammar?
development1-q02.simple: Some say children learn grammar only because adults reward correct sentences. Which finding argues most clearly against that?

development1-q03.college: Why did categorical perception initially seem compelling as evidence for a language-specific perceptual mechanism?
development1-q03.simple: Why did categorical perception (hearing sounds in sharp groups) at first look like proof of a special language system?

development1-q04.college: In an infant habituation paradigm, which comparison best isolates discrimination from a general increase in responding?
development1-q04.simple: In a baby habituation study (the baby gets used to a sound), which comparison best shows the baby noticed a change and is not just getting more active?

development1-q05.college: Why equate the acoustic magnitude of within-category and between-category VOT changes?
development1-q05.simple: Why make the VOT change (delay before voicing) the same size inside a sound group and across two groups?

development1-q06.college: Why did Eimas's infant findings encourage nativist interest without, on their own, demonstrating language specificity?
development1-q06.simple: Why did Eimas's baby results make people think of inborn abilities, yet not prove a special language system?

development1-q07.college: Younger English-learning infants discriminate a nonnative contrast better than older English-learning infants. Which additional comparison would best identify language-specific tuning?
development1-q07.simple: Younger English-learning babies hear a foreign sound difference better than older English-learning babies. What extra group would best show that their own language is doing the tuning?

development1-q08.college: What initial perceptual state does a pure selection account, in which infants select from universal contrasts, predict?
development1-q08.simple: One idea says babies start with all possible sound differences and keep only some. What does it say babies can hear at the start?

development1-q09.college: Which pair of findings most directly challenges the claims that categorical perception is exclusive to speech and exclusive to humans?
development1-q09.simple: Which two findings best argue against the ideas that hearing sounds in sharp groups happens only for speech and only in humans?

development1-q10.college: Adults discriminate equal-sized nonspeech differences best across the pluck and bow boundary. Which inference is warranted?
development1-q10.simple: Adults hear equal-sized differences in sounds that are not speech best at the line between pluck and bow. What can we fairly conclude?

development1-q11.college: Infant sucking recovers for between-category nonspeech changes but not for matched within-category changes. What does this comparison indicate?
development1-q11.simple: Babies suck harder again when a non-speech sound crosses into a new group, but not for an equal change inside one group. What does this show?

development1-q12.college: In the chinchilla training procedure, what does the discriminative stimulus (SD) signal to the animal?
development1-q12.simple: In the chinchilla training, what does the SD (the cue signal) tell the animal?

development1-q13.college: Young infants discriminate /ma/ from /na/ but do not discriminate /na/ from /ŋa/ comparably well. Which claim does this weaken?
development1-q13.simple: Young babies can tell /ma/ from /na/ but have a harder time telling /na/ from /ŋa/. Which idea does this weaken?

development1-q14.college: Filipino-learning infants become better at the difficult nasal contrast with age. Which process must be added to a narrowing account based solely on loss?
development1-q14.simple: Filipino-learning babies get better at the hard nasal sound difference as they grow. What must be added to the idea that babies only lose sound differences?

development1-q15.college: In the associative learning example, why can a bell eventually come to influence salivation?
development1-q15.simple: In the learning-by-pairing example, why can a bell end up causing drooling (salivation)?

development1-q16.college: What information does a statistical vowel learner extract from a distribution of tokens in F1 by F2 space?
development1-q16.simple: A statistical learner hears many vowel sounds spread out on an F1 and F2 chart. What does it pick up from that spread?

development1-q17.college: In Maye's study, test tokens 3 and 6 were presented equally often during familiarization in both groups. Why is this design feature important?
development1-q17.simple: In Maye's study, test sounds 3 and 6 were played the same number of times for both groups. Why does that matter?

development1-q18.college: Following bimodal or unimodal familiarization, only one group discriminates alternating from repeated test tokens. Which result is consistent with distributional learning?
development1-q18.simple: One group heard sounds bunched in two humps (bimodal), the other in one hump (unimodal). Only one group then tells switching sounds from repeated sounds. What result fits learning from how sounds are spread out?

development1-q19.college: Live Mandarin exposure yields clearer learning than audio-only or television exposure. Which factor does this comparison emphasize?
development1-q19.simple: Babies learn Mandarin sounds better from a live person than from audio or TV. What does this comparison point to?

development1-q20.college: Which statement best characterizes constrained statistical learning?
development1-q20.simple: Which statement best describes statistical learning that has limits on what it picks up?

development2-q01.college: Why is speech segmentation not equivalent to dividing the signal at silent intervals?
development2-q01.simple: Why can't we find words in speech just by cutting at the quiet gaps?

development2-q02.college: After familiarization, infants recognize kingdom in passages more readily than device. Which segmentation cue does this implicate?
development2-q02.simple: After hearing both words, babies spot kingdom in a story more easily than device. Which cue for finding words is at work?

development2-q03.college: A sound sequence that rarely occurs within words appears in connected speech. How can phonotactic knowledge aid segmentation?
development2-q03.simple: Two sounds that rarely sit together inside a word show up side by side in speech. How can phonotactic knowledge (knowing which sound orders are allowed) help?

development2-q04.college: Why divide the frequency of a syllable pair by the frequency of its first syllable?
development2-q04.simple: Why compare how often a pair of syllables occurs with how often its first syllable occurs?

development2-q05.college: What point about segmentation cues do ice cream and I scream illustrate?
development2-q05.simple: What do ice cream and I scream show about finding word edges in speech?

development2-q06.college: Why did Saffran's experiment use monotone, continuous streams of CV syllables?
development2-q06.simple: Why did Saffran play flat-sounding, nonstop strings of CV syllables (a consonant then a vowel)?

development2-q07.college: The artificial speech stream contains no pauses, yet syllables within words reliably predict one another. What can a statistical learner extract?
development2-q07.simple: The made-up speech has no gaps, but syllables inside each word always come in the same order. What can a learner who tracks patterns pick up?

development2-q08.college: A color-coded printout reveals the artificial words in the stream. Why should the colors not be regarded as a cue available to infants?
development2-q08.simple: A printout uses colors to mark the made-up words. Why should the colors not count as a cue the babies had?

development2-q09.college: A trained word and a part-word spanning a word boundary occur with equal frequency. What is the purpose of comparing them?
development2-q09.simple: A learned word and a part-word (pieces of two words joined across the edge) were heard the same number of times. Why compare them?

development2-q10.college: GOPILA and BU-GIKO each occur twice, but GI follows BU on only some occurrences of BU. Which quantity differs?
development2-q10.simple: GOPILA and BU-GIKO are each heard twice, but GI comes after BU only some of the times BU is heard. What is different?

development2-q11.college: At test, infants attend longer to part-words than to frequency-matched trained words. What does this novelty preference indicate?
development2-q11.simple: At test, babies listen longer to part-words than to learned words heard just as often. What does this preference for the new-seeming item show?

development2-q12.college: Why does hearing cat in the presence of an animal fail to determine the word's meaning uniquely?
development2-q12.simple: Why does hearing cat near an animal not tell a child exactly what the word means?

development2-q13.college: Beyond two people simply viewing the same object, what does joint attention contribute?
development2-q13.simple: What does joint attention give a child that two people just looking at the same thing does not?

development2-q14.college: Infants learn a label produced by an interacting adult but not one produced by a voice behind a screen, even while handling the object. Which simple account is weakened?
development2-q14.simple: Babies learn a name from an adult who plays with them, but not from a hidden voice behind a screen, even when they hold the toy. Which simple idea does this weaken?

development2-q15.college: An adult looks into a bucket while labeling a toy other than the one the infant is holding. What distinguishes using the speaker's intention from a self-focused association?
development2-q15.simple: An adult looks into a bucket while naming a toy that is not the one the baby is holding. What would show the baby uses the speaker's intention instead of a self-focused association (linking the word to whatever the baby is focused on)?

development2-q16.college: In Akhtar's task, the adult's emotional expression helps infants determine a novel word's referent. What inference does this require?
development2-q16.simple: In Akhtar's task, the adult's facial reaction helps babies work out what a new word names. What kind of reasoning is the baby using?

development2-q17.college: A novel noun is used in the presence of an unfamiliar object with an unusual handle. What does the whole-object assumption initially favor?
development2-q17.simple: A new noun is said near a strange object with an odd handle. What does the whole-object assumption (a default guess children make about new nouns) favor at first?

development2-q18.college: A familiar dog and an unfamiliar object are both present when a novel label is requested. Which choice does mutual exclusivity predict?
development2-q18.simple: A known dog and an unknown object are both there. Someone uses a new word and asks for the thing it names. What does mutual exclusivity (the idea that each thing has only one name) predict?

development2-q19.college: Why is the utterance mommy up insufficient on its own to demonstrate an adult-like productive construction?
development2-q19.simple: Why does a child saying mommy up not prove, by itself, that the child has an adult-like grammar pattern?

development2-q20.college: Children match the duck is gorping the bunny to a novel action in which the duck acts on the bunny. Why use a novel verb?
development2-q20.simple: Children match the duck is gorping the bunny to a new action where the duck does something to the bunny. Why use a made-up verb?

l1-critical-q01.college: Adults improve with intensive training, although early learning is easier. Which developmental timing account best accommodates both findings?
l1-critical-q01.simple: Adults get better with hard training, but learning is easier early in life. Which timing idea fits both facts?

l1-critical-q02.college: After a childhood cataract is surgically corrected, vision in the affected eye remains poor. What accounts for the persistent deficit?
l1-critical-q02.simple: A child's cloudy lens (cataract) is fixed, but that eye still sees poorly. Why does the problem stay?

l1-critical-q03.college: In the amblyopia account, what does colonization by the stronger eye mean?
l1-critical-q03.simple: In the lazy-eye account, what does it mean that the better eye takes over (colonizes)?

l1-critical-q04.college: What is the rationale for patching the stronger eye instead of allowing continued reliance on it?
l1-critical-q04.simple: Why cover the better eye with a patch instead of letting the child keep using it?

l1-critical-q05.college: What does perceptual learning in adults with amblyopia indicate about an early optimal window?
l1-critical-q05.simple: What does practice-based learning in adults with a lazy eye (amblyopia) show about an early best time for learning?

l1-critical-q06.college: Which sequence best summarizes the amblyopia example?
l1-critical-q06.simple: Which order of events best sums up the lazy-eye example?

l1-critical-q07.college: In a deaf child's history, why distinguish accessible language input from mere exposure to speech sounds?
l1-critical-q07.simple: For a deaf child, why does it matter whether language was truly usable, not just whether speech sounds were around?

l1-critical-q08.simple: What led Lenneberg to say language learning depends on the brain growing up?

l1-critical-q09.college: Why does a large age gap in the postmortem brain data matter?
l1-critical-q09.simple: Why is a big gap in ages among the brains studied after death a problem?

l1-critical-q10.college: Why were outcomes after childhood hemispherectomy relevant to accounts based on cerebral dominance?
l1-critical-q10.simple: Why did results from children who had half the brain removed (hemispherectomy) matter for ideas about one side of the brain taking over language?

l1-critical-q11.college: Children with perinatal stroke outperform comparable adults but may remain in the low-normal range. Which conclusion is consistent with both observations?
l1-critical-q11.simple: Children who had a stroke around birth do better than adults with similar strokes, but may still score at the low end of normal. What conclusion fits both facts?

l1-critical-q12.college: Why analyze Genie's vocabulary and grammar separately instead of reporting a single language score?
l1-critical-q12.simple: Why look at Genie's words and grammar one at a time instead of giving one overall language score?

l1-critical-q13.college: Genie acquired many words and some comprehension of plurals. Which possibility does this rule out?
l1-critical-q13.simple: Genie learned many words and came to understand some plurals. What does this rule out?

l1-critical-q14.college: Why should Genie's production deficit not be taken as a direct index of her vocabulary knowledge?
l1-critical-q14.simple: Why shouldn't Genie's trouble speaking be read as simply showing how many words she knew?

l1-critical-q15.college: Which pattern in Genie's development specifically motivated an interpretation based on the timing of first-language grammar?
l1-critical-q15.simple: What pattern in Genie's learning made people think grammar in a first language has a time limit?

l1-critical-q16.college: Two groups begin ASL late, one with an early spoken first language and one with no accessible early language. Why is this contrast important?
l1-critical-q16.simple: Two groups start ASL late. One group had a spoken first language early. The other had no usable language early. Why is this comparison important?

l1-critical-q17.college: Late learners of sign as a second language outperform late learners of sign as a first language. Which explanation does this support?
l1-critical-q17.simple: People who learn sign late as a second language do better than people who learn sign late as their first language. Which explanation does this back up?

l1-critical-q18.college: If withholding a first language does not preserve child-like acquisition ability later, which simple hypothesis is weakened?
l1-critical-q18.simple: If keeping a child from any first language does not save a child-like ability to learn later, which simple idea is weakened?

l1-critical-q19.college: Which claim best summarizes the first-language evidence?
l1-critical-q19.simple: Which statement best sums up what the first-language cases show?

l1-critical-q20.college: How does adult visual learning refine the discussion of a critical period for language?
l1-critical-q20.simple: How do results on adults learning to see better sharpen the debate about a critical period (a time limit) for language?

sentence-q01.college: For the horse raced past the barn fell, what is the correct structural analysis?
sentence-q01.simple: In the horse raced past the barn fell, what does the sentence actually mean once it is read correctly?

sentence-q02.college: Why do garden-path sentences provide evidence for incremental processing?
sentence-q02.simple: How do garden-path sentences (sentences that lead you the wrong way) show that we interpret words as they come?

sentence-q03.college: A parser following minimal attachment encounters a locally ambiguous reduced relative clause. Which initial analysis does it prefer?
sentence-q03.simple: A parser that follows minimal attachment (choose the simplest structure) meets a reduced relative that could be read two ways. Which reading does it pick first?

sentence-q04.college: In the burglar blew open the safe with the dynamite, what role does the preferred verb-phrase attachment assign to dynamite?
sentence-q04.simple: In the burglar blew open the safe with the dynamite, the favored reading links with the dynamite to the action. What does that make the dynamite?

sentence-q05.college: Why is the version ending in with the jewels more difficult in the matching safe sentence?
sentence-q05.simple: Why is the safe sentence that ends with the jewels harder to read?

sentence-q06.college: Which finding is most problematic for a strictly syntax-first model of initial parsing?
sentence-q06.simple: Which finding causes the most trouble for the idea that grammar alone sets the first reading of a sentence?

sentence-q07.college: Many reduced relative clauses are easy to process when semantics and usage favor them. What does the constraint-based account conclude from this?
sentence-q07.simple: Many reduced relatives are easy to read when meaning and common use point toward them. What does the constraint-based account (many cues work together) conclude?

sentence-q08.college: Why might the burglar arrested in the parking lot be easier to process than the matching policeman sentence?
sentence-q08.simple: Why might the burglar arrested in the parking lot be easier to read than the same sentence with policeman?

sentence-q09.college: In the one-apple display, why are fixations on the empty towel informative?
sentence-q09.simple: In the scene with one apple, why do looks at the empty towel tell us something?

sentence-q10.college: Adding a second apple makes on the towel useful for identifying which apple is meant. Which eye-movement pattern is expected?
sentence-q10.simple: With a second apple added, on the towel now helps tell which apple is meant. What pattern of looking should follow?

sentence-q11.college: In the one-apple and two-apple comparison, which factor is held constant, making the contextual effect important?
sentence-q11.simple: In the one-apple and two-apple test, what stays the same that makes the effect of the scene matter?

sentence-q12.college: A mouse-tracking trajectory curves toward an incorrect destination before reaching the correct one. What does the trajectory reveal beyond endpoint accuracy?
sentence-q12.simple: A mouse path bends toward a wrong spot before ending at the right one. What does the path show that the final click does not?

sentence-q13.college: What does time-locking an ERP to a particular word allow researchers to determine?
sentence-q13.simple: What can researchers learn by lining up the ERP (brain wave recording) to the moment a word appears?

sentence-q14.college: Why is eaten disruptive in the pizza was in the eaten?
sentence-q14.simple: Why does eaten cause trouble in the pizza was in the eaten?

sentence-q15.college: What does the early latency of the ELAN most directly establish?
sentence-q15.simple: What does the fast timing of the ELAN (an early brain response) most directly show?

sentence-q16.college: Through what mechanism can a syntactic expectation influence early visual processing?
sentence-q16.simple: How can expecting a certain kind of word change early seeing of the word?

sentence-q17.college: Perches functions as a noun in one sentence and as a verb in another. What makes this useful experimentally?
sentence-q17.simple: Perches is a noun in one sentence and a verb in another. Why is that useful in an experiment?

sentence-q18.college: Perches looks relatively noun-like in form but is used as a verb. Which research question follows from form-prediction accounts?
sentence-q18.simple: Perches looks a lot like a noun but is used as a verb. What question do form-prediction accounts (the idea that the brain predicts how the next word will look or sound from its expected category) raise?

sentence-q19.college: An early effect occurs for violations with strongly noun-like forms but not for neutral nouns. Which account does this support?
sentence-q19.simple: An early brain effect shows up for very noun-looking words in the wrong spot, but not for plain nouns. Which idea does this back up?

sentence-q20.college: Which pairing correctly matches an example sentence with its central lesson?
sentence-q20.simple: Which pair correctly matches an example sentence with its main point?

l2-learning-q01.college: An adult acquires initial L2 vocabulary rapidly but does not attain native-like proficiency later. Why are these findings not contradictory?
l2-learning-q01.simple: An adult learns first words in a second language fast but never ends up sounding native. Why is that not a contradiction?

l2-learning-q02.college: Why might older L2 learners benefit from already understanding events and spatial relations?
l2-learning-q02.simple: Why can it help older second-language learners that they already understand events and where things are?

l2-learning-q03.college: Under what condition does reusing an L1 representation constitute negative transfer?
l2-learning-q03.simple: When does using something from your first language count as negative transfer (carrying over something that hurts)?

l2-learning-q04.college: English listeners assimilate Hindi dental and retroflex stops to a single familiar category. Which learning problem results?
l2-learning-q04.simple: English listeners hear Hindi dental and retroflex stops as one familiar English sound. What learning problem does that cause?

l2-learning-q05.college: Why might classifiers pose difficulty for an English-speaking learner of Chinese beyond memorizing a new form?
l2-learning-q05.simple: Why can classifiers (counting words tied to nouns) be hard for an English speaker learning Chinese, beyond just memorizing a new word?

l2-learning-q06.college: Two French synonyms carry different grammatical genders. What must the learner keep distinct?
l2-learning-q06.simple: Two French words mean the same thing but have different grammatical genders. What does the learner need to keep apart?

l2-learning-q07.college: Why can cognates facilitate early L2 learning?
l2-learning-q07.simple: Why can cognates (words that look and sound alike across languages) help early learning?

l2-learning-q08.college: A learner interprets embarazado by way of English embarrassed. Which process produces this error?
l2-learning-q08.simple: A learner reads embarazado as English embarrassed. What causes this mistake?

l2-learning-q09.college: Why use invented, foreign-like forms in a paired-associate learning task?
l2-learning-q09.simple: In a word-pair learning task, why use made-up words that sound foreign?

l2-learning-q10.college: Cognate-like pairs are acquired faster and recalled better a week later. What does this pattern support?
l2-learning-q10.simple: Pairs that look like cognates are learned faster and remembered better a week later. What does this show?

l2-learning-q11.college: Why is producing a new form more diagnostic than only recognizing its familiar meaning?
l2-learning-q11.simple: Why does making a new word yourself tell us more than just picking out what it means?

l2-learning-q12.college: A results table shows both a concreteness advantage and a cognate advantage. Why should these effects be kept distinct?
l2-learning-q12.simple: A table shows an advantage for concrete words and an advantage for cognates. Why should these not be lumped together?

l2-learning-q13.college: What defines an onset cohort competitor?
l2-learning-q13.simple: What makes a word an onset cohort competitor (one kind of rival word)?

l2-learning-q14.college: For Russian and English bilingual listeners, why can matches compete with the English target speaker?
l2-learning-q14.simple: For people who speak Russian and English, why can matches compete with the English word speaker?

l2-learning-q15.college: In the English task, competitors with overlapping Russian names draw fixations above control levels, even alongside an English competitor. What follows?
l2-learning-q15.simple: In the English task, objects whose Russian names start like the target get more looks than control objects, even with an English rival on screen. What does this show?

l2-learning-q16.college: In the Russian task, the English competitor's small advantage is not statistically reliable. How should this result be reported?
l2-learning-q16.simple: In the Russian task, the English rival gets a small edge, but it is not statistically reliable. How should this be described?

l2-learning-q17.college: In the bilingual lexicon model, which configuration of connections accounts for stronger L1 influence during L2 processing?
l2-learning-q17.simple: In the model of two-language memory, which set of links explains why the first language pulls harder while using the second?

l2-learning-q18.college: Why does balanced bilingualism not necessarily imply two separate monolingual systems?
l2-learning-q18.simple: Why does being equally good in two languages not mean having two separate one-language systems?

l2-learning-q19.college: Korean adoptees perform like monolingual French listeners on the tested Korean contrasts. What can be concluded?
l2-learning-q19.simple: Korean adoptees score like French-only listeners on the Korean sound differences tested. What can we conclude?

l2-learning-q20.college: When comparing adoptees with childhood overhearers, why consider differences in ongoing language exposure?
l2-learning-q20.simple: Why look at how much each group kept hearing the language when comparing adoptees with people who overheard it as children?

l2-sensitive-q01.college: According to Lenneberg's cerebral-dominance account, what factor is relevant to a window for language learning?
l2-sensitive-q01.simple: In Lenneberg's account of one brain side taking charge, what matters for the time window for learning language?

l2-sensitive-q02.college: What makes L2 learners useful for research on age of acquisition?
l2-sensitive-q02.simple: Why are second-language learners useful for studying how the age you start affects learning?

l2-sensitive-q03.college: In Johnson and Newport's research question, what does ultimate attainment refer to?
l2-sensitive-q03.simple: In Johnson and Newport's question, what does ultimate attainment (final skill level) mean?

l2-sensitive-q04.college: Participants listen to sentences and make untimed grammaticality judgments. Which type of knowledge might this procedure particularly encourage?
l2-sensitive-q04.simple: People hear sentences and decide, with no time limit, whether each is grammatical. What kind of knowledge might this let them lean on?

l2-sensitive-q05.college: Why analyze early and late arrival ranges separately instead of reporting a single overall correlation?
l2-sensitive-q05.simple: Why look at early and late arrivals one group at a time instead of giving one overall correlation?

l2-sensitive-q06.college: In the scatterplot, what does it mean for accuracy among late arrivals to be nearly random?
l2-sensitive-q06.simple: In the scatterplot, what does it mean that scores for late arrivals look almost random?

l2-sensitive-q07.college: Which result belongs to the early-arrival pattern in Johnson and Newport's data?
l2-sensitive-q07.simple: Which result is part of what Johnson and Newport found for people who arrived young?

l2-sensitive-q08.college: Why does the sensitive-period interpretation consider both the early slope and the later scatter?
l2-sensitive-q08.simple: Why does the sensitive-period idea care about both the early downward trend and the later spread of scores?

l2-sensitive-q09.college: Under the exercise hypothesis, what should successful early L1 acquisition protect?
l2-sensitive-q09.simple: The exercise hypothesis says using language early keeps something in shape. What should learning a first language early protect?

l2-sensitive-q10.college: Older learners acquired an L1 early yet show lower L2 attainment. Which hypothesis is more directly consistent with this?
l2-sensitive-q10.simple: Older learners had a first language early in life but still end up worse at a second language. Which idea fits this better?

l2-sensitive-q11.college: A learner can state an English grammatical rule correctly but struggles to apply it in spontaneous speech. Which distinction does this illustrate?
l2-sensitive-q11.simple: A learner can explain an English rule correctly but has trouble using it when talking freely. What difference does this show?

l2-sensitive-q12.college: Untimed GJT scores correlate strongly with years of formal L2 instruction. Why is this significant?
l2-sensitive-q12.simple: Scores on the untimed GJT (grammar judgment test) go up strongly with years of second-language classes. Why does that matter?

l2-sensitive-q13.college: At comparable arrival ages, why might Spanish and English learners differ from Chinese or Korean and English learners?
l2-sensitive-q13.simple: Why might Spanish speakers learning English do differently from Chinese or Korean speakers learning English, even when they arrived at the same age?

l2-sensitive-q14.college: Late L2 learners handle questions relatively well, even though children acquire questions late in L1. Which assumption is weakened?
l2-sensitive-q14.simple: Late learners do fairly well with questions, even though children learn questions late in their first language. Which idea does this weaken?

l2-sensitive-q15.college: Why might English determiners be particularly difficult for a learner whose L1 has no comparable system?
l2-sensitive-q15.simple: Why might English words like the and a be extra hard for someone whose first language has nothing like them?

l2-sensitive-q16.college: A different L1 group shows a different distribution of AOA and attainment. What must a general maturational explanation also account for?
l2-sensitive-q16.simple: A group with a different first language shows a different link between AOA (age of arrival) and final skill. What else must a brain-growth explanation explain?

l2-sensitive-q17.college: Why is age of arrival not automatically a pure index of maturational capacity?
l2-sensitive-q17.simple: Why isn't the age someone arrived a clean measure of how ready their brain was to learn?

l2-sensitive-q18.college: An untimed judgment test and spontaneous conversation produce different relationships with age. Which interpretation is most productive?
l2-sensitive-q18.simple: An untimed grammar test and free conversation show different links with age. What is the most useful way to read this?

l2-sensitive-q19.college: Which summary is best supported by the research on sensitive periods in L2 acquisition?
l2-sensitive-q19.simple: Which summary best fits the research on time windows for learning a second language?

l2-sensitive-q20.college: How does difficulty with a late L2 after an early L1 complicate a simple interpretation of the delayed-L1 evidence?
l2-sensitive-q20.simple: People who had a first language early still struggle with a second language learned late. How does that change a simple reading of the late-first-language cases?
